facts: A normal distribution is **symmetrical**: the left and right halves are mirror images about the centre.
The mean, median and mode of a theoretical normal distribution are exactly equal and sit at the centre; in observed data from a normal distribution, they are approximately equal.
Most of the data sits near the centre, and the frequencies decrease steadily towards both **tails**.
A **skewed** display has one longer tail, so it is not normal even though it has a single peak.
A display with two peaks is **bimodal**, and a flat display has no peak; neither shape is normal.
Real data is rarely a perfect bell, so 'approximately normal' is enough when the shape is close.
On two normal curves drawn on the same scale, the curve whose peak is further right has the larger mean.
A wider, flatter curve has the larger standard deviation; a taller, narrower curve has the smaller one.
steps: Check the display is roughly symmetrical
Check there is a single central peak with the frequencies falling away on both sides
Check the mean, median and mode are approximately equal

workedExamples.solution_text:
Dataset A could be normally distributed. Its frequencies match on either side of $4$ and decrease towards both tails, giving a symmetrical display with a single central peak.

Dataset B is not normally distributed. Its peak is at the left end, and its tail extends to the right. It is positively skewed rather than symmetrical.

workedExamples.question_text:
Each row gives the frequencies for scores $2$ to $8$. Decide whether each dataset could be normally distributed. Give reasons.

| Dataset / Score | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 2 | 6 | 11 | 16 | 12 | 5 | 2 |
| B | 6 | 6 | 6 | 6 | 6 | 6 | 6 |
| C | 2 | 7 | 12 | 4 | 12 | 7 | 2 |
| D | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 | 8 | 14 | 7 |
workedExamples.solution_text:
A could be normally distributed. The frequencies rise to one central peak at $5$ and fall away on both sides. Matching frequencies are close, so the display is approximately symmetrical.

B is flat: every score has frequency $6$. It has no single central peak, so it is not normally distributed.

C is symmetrical, but it has two peaks at $4$ and $6$, with a dip at $5$. It is bimodal rather than bell-shaped, so it is not normally distributed.

D has a peak near the right end at $7$ and a longer tail towards the lower scores. It is negatively skewed rather than symmetrical, so it is not normally distributed.

workedExamples.question_text:
The table shows the scores of $40$ students.

| Score | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 | 10 | 11 | 12 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Frequency | 2 | 5 | 8 | 10 | 8 | 5 | 2 |

Calculate the mean, median and mode. Use the averages and the shape to justify whether the data is approximately normally distributed.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}\text{Mean}&=\frac{6(2)+7(5)+8(8)+9(10)+10(8)+11(5)+12(2)}{40}\\&=\frac{360}{40}\\&=9\end{aligned}$

The cumulative frequencies are $2$, $7$, $15$, $25$, $33$, $38$, $40$. The $20$th and $21$st scores are both $9$, so the median is $9$.

The highest frequency is $10$, occurring at score $9$, so the mode is $9$.

The mean, median and mode are all $9$. The frequencies are symmetrical about $9$, rise to a single central peak and fall away towards both tails. The data could be approximately normally distributed.

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Frequency | 2 | 5 | 10 | 6 | 10 | 5 | 2 |

Sam says, “The mean and median are both $9$, and the frequencies are symmetrical, so the data must be normally distributed.” Check the mean and median, then explain why Sam's conclusion is wrong.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}\text{Mean}&=\frac{6(2)+7(5)+8(10)+9(6)+10(10)+11(5)+12(2)}{40}\\&=\frac{360}{40}\\&=9\end{aligned}$

The cumulative frequencies are $2$, $7$, $17$, $23$, $33$, $38$, $40$. The $20$th and $21$st scores are both $9$, so the median is $9$.

The frequencies are symmetrical about $9$, but the two peaks are at $8$ and $10$, each with frequency $10$. The centre has a lower frequency of $6$.

A normal distribution needs a single central peak as well as symmetry. This display is bimodal, so Sam's conclusion is wrong.

(a) Curve $C$ has the largest mean. Its peak is furthest to the right, and a normal curve's mean lies beneath its peak.

(b) Curve $B$ has the largest standard deviation. It is the widest and flattest curve, so its values are the most spread out.

(c) Curves $A$ and $B$ have the same mean. Their peaks lie at the same horizontal position.

(d) Curves $A$ and $C$ have the same standard deviation. Their widths match; moving a curve horizontally changes its mean without changing its spread.

The mean, median and mode are all $7$, and the frequencies are symmetrical about $7$ with a single central peak, so the data is approximately normally distributed.

The table shows the number of days per week that each of $49$ adults exercised.
$\begin{array}{c|ccccccc} \text{Days} & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 2 & 3 & 4 & 30 & 6 & 2 & 2 \end{array}$
Riley says, "The mean, median and mode are all $4$, so this data must be normally distributed." Show that Riley's three averages are correct, and explain why his conclusion is wrong.
mastery.solution_text:
$\text{Mean} = \dfrac{1(2)+2(3)+3(4)+4(30)+5(6)+6(2)+7(2)}{49}$
$= \dfrac{196}{49}$
$= 4$
The $25$th value is the middle one of $49$, and the running totals are $2$, $5$, $9$, $39$, so the median is $4$.
The largest frequency is $30$, so the mode is $4$.
Equal averages are not enough: the frequencies either side of $4$ are $2$, $3$, $4$ on the left and $6$, $2$, $2$ on the right, so the display is not symmetrical.
The display is also a single sharp spike rather than a bell that falls away gradually, so the data is not normally distributed.

Curve $B$ is the widest and flattest of the three, so its values are the most spread out.
Curve $B$ has the largest standard deviation.

mastery.question_text:
The table shows the scores of $48$ students on a test.
$\begin{array}{c|ccccccc} \text{Score} & 28 & 30 & 32 & 34 & 36 & 38 & 40 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 2 & 7 & 12 & 6 & 12 & 7 & 2 \end{array}$
A student says, "The frequencies are symmetrical about $34$, so this data must be approximately normally distributed."
Use the frequency data to explain why the student's conclusion is wrong.
mastery.solution_text:
The frequencies are symmetrical about $34$: matching values on either side have frequencies $12$, $7$, $2$.
However, there are two peaks at $32$ and $36$, each with frequency $12$, and a dip at $34$ with frequency $6$.
Symmetry alone is not enough: a normal distribution must also have a single central peak.
This display is bimodal rather than bell-shaped, so the data is not approximately normally distributed.
